original_script: There is a hole in your vision right now, and you almost never notice it. Inside each eye, light lands on a retina packed with cells that detect it. But one small spot has no visual cells at all. That is where the optic nerve leaves the eye, carrying signals toward the brain. Close one eye during a dot test, and the missing mark can disappear completely. Your brain fills the gap from the surrounding pattern. Seeing is partly reconstruction.

storyboard.caption: LIGHT → RETINA

storyboard.visual: The retinal surface reveals one small optic-disc region without photoreceptor markers while surrounding cells remain dense
storyboard.caption: NO VISUAL CELLS HERE

storyboard.visual: Same eye model rotates slightly as signal paths converge and leave through the optic nerve toward an abstract brain silhouette
storyboard.caption: THE OPTIC NERVE EXIT

storyboard.visual: Minimal original dot-and-cross demonstration in the same charcoal studio; the dot naturally disappears at one viewing position
storyboard.caption: TRY THE DOT TEST

storyboard.visual: Return to the same hazel eye as the surrounding studio reflection flows smoothly across the blind-spot region; restrained amber highlight marks the reveal
storyboard.caption: SEEING IS RECONSTRUCTION

factual_notes.claim: Photoreceptors in the retina convert light into electrical signals that travel through the optic nerve to the brain.
factual_notes.source_title: How the Eyes Work — National Eye Institute

factual_notes.claim: The physiological blind spot corresponds to the location where the optic nerve exits and visual cells are absent.
factual_notes.source_title: National Eye Institute glossary — blind spot

factual_notes.claim: Perceptual filling-in can make the visual system fill the informational void at the blind spot using surrounding content.
factual_notes.source_title: Predictive Coding: A Possible Explanation of Filling-In at the Blind Spot
